title: Concerning the Way to Govern Cities or Principalities Which Lived Under Their Own Laws Before They Were Annexed
coreMove: Treat remembered liberty as an active rallying force that ordinary benefits will not erase.
sourcePressure: The source says annexed cities accustomed to their own laws and freedom can be held by ruin, residence, or tribute through a dependent oligarchy, but their watchword of liberty and ancient privileges remains a permanent danger. Places accustomed to a prince are easier because the old family can be removed and people do not know how to make a new ruler among themselves.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version becomes an anti-democracy claim or simple repression advice. The writer must focus on the operational problem of holding a free city whose memory of liberty can organize rebellion long after conquest.

hook: a modern partisan argument about democracy
a conqueror deciding whether to be merciful in the abstract
counterintuition: most people assume time heals conquest, but actually memory survives
benefits never matter to free people
destruction is the only lesson of the chapter
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds and list freedoms you value
write about a time you resisted authority
choose whether you would ruin or spare a city
examples: neighborhood association resisting a zoning change

exampleSpecs.domain: an annexed maritime republic whose council hall still displays its old voting shells
exampleSpecs.audience: a governor considering tribute through a friendly merchant council
exampleSpecs.stakes: tax revenue may flow for a year, but the old voting shells can become the symbol around which sailors and merchants rally
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The governor watches a dock boy touch the voting-shell case before reading a tribute notice, and realizes the object is not decoration but a live summons to the old republic.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: White voting shells sit in a glass case inside the council hall.

exampleSpecs.domain: a conquered university town that once elected its own magistrates under a medieval charter
exampleSpecs.audience: a resident commander deciding whether to leave lectures and courts under old rules
exampleSpecs.stakes: scholars may accept tribute, but the charter oath can turn a fee dispute into a liberty rebellion
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: When students begin chanting the charter oath outside the court door, the commander holds the key to his lodging and sees why residence alone will not quiet a free town if the old law remains a banner.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A parchment charter hangs above a locked university court door.

exampleSpecs.domain: a dismantled fortress commune whose exiled families preserve gate stones in a chapel
exampleSpecs.audience: a military historian explaining why rebuilding the walls revives more than masonry
exampleSpecs.stakes: the commune has no army, but each stone can restore the name of liberty as a rallying point
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The historian lays the gate stone rubbing beside a later rebellion banner and shows the same carved motto appearing after a hundred quiet years.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A charcoal rubbing of a gate stone lies beside a folded rebellion banner.

exampleSpecs.domain: a mountain canton forced into a larger realm after generations of town-meeting law
exampleSpecs.audience: a tax collector warned not to mistake quiet payment for obedience
exampleSpecs.stakes: the canton pays tribute while hiding the meeting horn that can summon every village to resist
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The collector predicts the paid tribute means peace, then hears the meeting horn from the ridge and sees the account book close without anyone taking a receipt.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A leather meeting horn rests under a stack of tribute receipts.

exampleSpecs.domain: an island court previously governed by elected jurors but now held by a mainland prince
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince deciding between local oligarchy and direct residence
exampleSpecs.stakes: a dependent oligarchy may keep the prince friendly only while islanders believe the old jury stones cannot be recovered
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: A juror turns over one black verdict stone in his palm while the prince's appointee explains tribute, making clear which memory the new oligarchy must suppress or serve.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Black verdict stones click in a wooden jury bowl.

exampleSpecs.domain: a former princely mining valley compared with a free mining city after both are annexed
exampleSpecs.audience: a royal inspector deciding why one district accepts rule and the other keeps plotting
exampleSpecs.stakes: the valley lacks a ruling family and cannot agree on a replacement, while the city has an old guild bell and privileges that can organize vengeance
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The inspector removes the dead prince's crest from the valley ledger, then fails to lift the guild bell from the city ledger because every miner's mark points back to it.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A silver guild bell sits beside a torn princely crest.

skillTargets: identify when old laws and liberties remain a live organizing memory after annexation
distinguish free cities from formerly princely cities in retention scenarios
analyze the three stated options: ruin, residence, or tribute through a dependent oligarchy
evaluate whether benefits, time, or partial autonomy would actually quiet a city with a liberty watchword

tryThisNowSpec: Find one conquered, annexed, or absorbed community in history. Write the old word, object, or privilege people could rally around, then test whether benefits alone would make that memory disappear.
